was free from unsatu- rated hydrocarbons (before the sulfuric acid absorption), and boiled at —23.5° C., which excluded the presence of any appreciable amount of saturated hydrocarbons.

props.name: ether formation greatly affected by time of contact

evidence.quote: The influence of time of contact is evident from the data of Table I for 350° C.
At space velocities of 3000 and 7500 the ether found was, respectively, 1.42 and 0.71 grams per pass.
Similarly, at 375° C. the production was 3.16 and 1.47 grams for the same respective space velocities.
the latter reaction in the case of zinc chro-
mate is greatly affected by the time of contact.
In the pres- sure synthesis of methanol the space velocities are relatively high and the time of contact short, thus favoring the methanol reaction and limiting the formation of ether.

props.statement: Ether formation over zinc chromate is greatly affected by time of contact: at 350 °C the ether found was 1.42 and 0.71 grams per pass at space velocities 3000 and 7500, and at 375 °C 3.16 and 1.47 grams; the high space velocities of the pressure synthesis favor the methanol reaction and limit ether formation.

props.name: CO conversion to methanol peaks near 375 °C at SV 3000

evidence.quote: At a space velocity of 3000 the conversion of the carbon monoxide to methanol was found to increase from about 7 per cent to a maxi- mum of about 30 per cent at 375 ° C. and then to decline to 20 per cent at 400° C.

props.statement: At a space velocity of 3000 the conversion of carbon monoxide to methanol over normal zinc chromate at 180 atmospheres increases from about 7 per cent to a maximum of about 30 per cent at 375 °C and then declines to 20 per cent at 400 °C.

props.name: dimethyl ether by-product increasing with temperature

evidence.quote: Dimethyl ether has been shown to be a by-product of the reaction, being formed from the methanol in amounts which increase with temperature between 300° and 400° C.
The data on the dimethyl ether produced between 300° and 400° C. as a by-product of the methanol synthesis (with nor- mal zinc chromate as the catalyst) are given in Table I.

props.statement: Dimethyl ether is a by-product of methanol synthesis over normal zinc chromate, formed from the methanol in amounts that increase with temperature between 300 and 400 °C.

props.name: ether formation has small effect on conversions

evidence.quote: The extent to which this ether formation affects the values for percentage conversions of carbon monoxide to methanol in Table I is not very great.

Under the experimental condi- tions employed, the formation of ether is slow compared with the methanol reaction, and if the carbon monoxide converted ultimately to ether is subtracted from the carbon monoxide which enters the catalyst chamber, the correction is about +0.6 per cent for the conversions in runs F and H and negli- gible in the others.

props.statement: Under the experimental conditions the formation of ether is slow compared with the methanol reaction; subtracting the CO converted to ether from the entering CO corrects the conversions by about +0.6 per cent in runs F and H and negligibly in the others.

props.name: gas identified as dimethyl ether

evidence.quote: In the tube a liquid was condensed, which proved to be largely dimethyl ether.
The perfect conformance of these characteristics with those of dimethyl ether fixed its identity fully.
The agreement is better than 3 parts in 1000, which represents approximately the accuracy of the apparatus and procedure, and it completes the identification of the ma- terial as dimethyl ether.

props.statement: The liquid condensed at -80 °C from the gases released by the synthetic methanol is largely dimethyl ether; its odor, boiling point (about -23.5 °C), solubility in sulfuric acid, density and molecular weight (46.17 vs 46.046) agree with dimethyl ether within 3 parts in 1000, fixing its identity.

props.name: ether formation unimportant for equilibrium determination at 1 atm

evidence.quote: If, in the absence of established equilib- rium values, we assume for the sake of discussion that Kp = at 300° C. = 60.6 X 10-t, then the ratio of CO to CH3OH (as CO) at 300° C. is 99.973 to 0.027;

The amount of ether that could be formed, although large with re- spect to the methanol, is yet so small that its influence on the ratio of carbon monoxide to methanol which measures the equilibrium is unimportant.

props.statement: At atmospheric pressure and 300 °C, with an assumed methanol equilibrium constant, the ether that could form, although large with respect to the methanol, is so small that its influence on the CO/methanol ratio measuring the equilibrium is unimportant.

props.name: indirect evidence of ether formation

evidence.quote: In addition to these theoretical considerations, there were several indirect evidences of ether formation.
One was the apparently large amount of gas set free by the methanol when it was drawn from the receiver under pressure into a receiver at room temperature and 1 atmosphere.

In those samples produced at 400° C. there was, in addition to a higher percentage of water, a corresponding increase in the amount of the crude methanol, which distilled slightly under the true boiling point of methanol.
A further indication was the fact that in the carbon monoxide balances there was an apparent
loss on the effluent side of the catalyst or among the products plus the residual carbon monoxide.

props.statement: Indirect evidences of ether formation were the large amount of gas set free when the methanol was let down from pressure, the distillation curves of methanol made at 400 °C (more water and more crude methanol distilling slightly below the boiling point of methanol, and volume loss), and an apparent carbon monoxide loss in the balances.

props.name: conversions at low space velocity above the estimated curve

evidence.quote: In Figure 1 the data from columns 2 and 5 of Table I have been plotted on the figure (No. 10) employed in the earlier paper2 to show the three values at 400° C. and a curve of estimated yields obtained by the Nernst approximation for- mula used empirically.
It is evident from these curves that the conversions, at low space
velocities and with side reac- tions excluded, would be greater than the “estimated” curve indicates.

props.statement: The experimental conversion curves for space velocities 3000 and 7500 show that at low space velocities and with side reactions excluded the conversions would be greater than the 'estimated' curve (Nernst approximation formula used empirically) indicates.

props.name: methanol catalysts much less active for ether formation

evidence.quote: In both cases the methanol catalysts (oxides) are highly active in the methanol reaction, which is rapid and much less active under the same conditions (as the writers’ experimental data on zinc chromate indicate) with respect to ether formation (re- action 1).
This represents the limit, and the actual conversion depends on the activity of the methanol catalyst employed and the time of contact.

props.statement: The methanol catalysts (oxides) are highly active in the rapid methanol reaction and much less active under the same conditions for ether formation, as the data on zinc chromate indicate; the equilibrium ether conversion (about 78-80 per cent of the methanol) is only a limit, the actual conversion depending on catalyst activity and time of contact.

props.name: methanol and ether lost in residual gas negligible

evidence.quote: The first test showed that the amounts of methanol vapors and methyl ether being lost in the residual

props.statement: The amounts of methanol vapor and methyl ether lost in the residual gas under the usual procedure were negligible.

It would mean that water gas under pressure passed over such a cata- lyst or catalysts would issue—reduced in volume, to be sure— but with a materially enhanced heating value due to the ether present in it and containing a recoverable quantity of methanol.
increasing the heating value of water gas by the catalytic forma- tion of dimethyl ether (which gasifies at —23.65° C.) seems to be á technical possibility.
